claim: The power of electrophysiologically measured cortical activity decays with an approximately 1/f function.
source: The power of electrophysiologically measured cortical activity decays with an approximately 1 /f function.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of electrophysiology and is supported by citations to prior work (Miller et al., 2009; Demanuele et al., 2007; Pritchard, 1992).

claim: The spectral exponent is modulated by various factors such as age, cognitive states or psychiatric/neurological disorders.
source: The slope of this decay (i.e. the spectral exponent, X X ) is modulated by various factors such as age, cognitive states or psychiatric/neurological disorders.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research showing these relationships.

claim: Similar effects for the spectral slope have been found in the electrocardiogram (ECG).
source: Interestingly, a mostly parallel line of research has also uncovered similar effects for the spectral slope in the electrocardiogram (ECG).
evidence: This is supported by citations to parallel research in cardiac physiology.

claim: The study analyzed a total of 1282 recordings of magnetoencephalography (MEG) resting state measurements with concurrent ECG in an age-diverse sample (18–88 years).
source: we analyzed a total of 1282 recordings of magnetoencephalography (MEG) resting state measurements with concurrent ECG in an age-diverse sample (18–88 years).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data analyzed in the study.

claim: The aperiodic signal recorded via surface electrodes/sensors originates from multiple physiological sources.
source: we demonstrate that the aperiodic signal recorded via surface electrodes/sensors originates from multiple physiological sources.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by the analyses presented.

claim: Common 'artifact' rejection approaches (i.e. ICA) may not be sufficient to separate cardiac from neural activity.
source: our results suggest that common 'artifact' rejection approaches (i.e. ICA) may not be sufficient to separate cardiac from neural activity.
evidence: This is supported by the temporal response function analysis showing residual ECG activity after ICA (Figure 3).

claim: Significant parts of age-related changes in aperiodic activity normally interpreted to be of neural origin can be explained by cardiac activity.
source: In particular, significant parts of age-related changes in aperiodic activity normally interpreted to be of neural origin can be explained by cardiac activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the regression analyses showing cardiac components explain age-related variance.

claim: Changes (flattening/steepening) of the spectral slope with age are dependent on the recording site and investigated frequency range.
source: Moreover, our results suggest that changes (flattening/steepening) of the spectral slope with age are dependent on the recording site and investigated frequency range.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis across different sensors and frequency ranges shown in Figure 4.

claim: Aperiodic neural activity is omnipresent in invasive recordings (e.g. ECoG).
source: Aperiodic neural activity is omnipresent both in invasive (e.g. ECoG Miller et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Miller et al., 2009.

claim: Aperiodic neural activity is omnipresent in non-invasive recordings (e.g. MEG/EEG).
source: and non-invasive (e.g. MEG/EEG Demanuele et al., 2007; Pritchard, 1992) recordings of electrophysiological brain activity
evidence: This is supported by citations to Demanuele et al., 2007 and Pritchard, 1992.

claim: Aperiodic activity is present in hemodynamic responses (e.g. fMRI).
source: and even in hemodynamic responses (e.g. fMRI He et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to He et al., 2010.

claim: In the frequency domain, when visualized in log-log coordinates, aperiodic activity manifests as a linear decay in power with an increase in frequency.
source: In the frequency domain, when visualized in log-log coordinates (log-frequency/log-power), aperiodic activity manifests as a linear decay in power with an increase in frequency (Miller et al., 2009)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Miller et al., 2009.

claim: Aperiodic neural activity is meaningfully modulated by age.
source: Several studies have shown that aperiodic neural activity is meaningfully modulated by various factors, such as age (Voytek et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Voytek et al., 2015.

claim: Aperiodic neural activity is meaningfully modulated by cognitive state (e.g. awake vs. sleep).
source: cognitive state (e.g. awake vs. sleep He et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to He et al., 2010.

claim: Aperiodic neural activity is meaningfully modulated by disorders like Parkinson's disease and epilepsy.
source: and disorders like Parkinson's disease and epilepsy (Ghinda et al., 2020; Mostile et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ghinda et al., 2020 and Mostile et al., 2019.

claim: Aperiodic activity is part of cardiac activity measured using electrocardiography (ECG).
source: However, aperiodic activity is not only present in recordings of neural activity, but also part of other physiological signals such as cardiac and muscle activity, commonly measured using electrocardiography (ECG Saul et al., 1988)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Saul et al., 1988.

claim: Aperiodic activity is part of muscle activity measured using electromyography.
source: and electromyography (Kozhemiako et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kozhemiako et al., 2022.

claim: Aperiodic activity measured using ECG is modulated by aging.
source: aperiodic activity measured using ECG (often referred to as power law or 1/f activity) is modulated by similar factors as neural aperiodic activity, including aging (Beckers et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Beckers et al., 2006.

claim: Aperiodic activity measured using ECG is modulated by different cognitive states (e.g. awake vs. sleep).
source: different cognitive states (e.g. awake vs. sleep Kozhemiako et al., 2022; Penzel et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kozhemiako et al., 2022 and Penzel et al., 2003.

claim: Aperiodic activity measured using ECG is modulated by disorders such as Parkinson's disease and epilepsy.
source: and disorders such as Parkinson's disease and epilepsy (Ansakorpi et al., 2002; Haapaniemi et al., 2001
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ansakorpi et al., 2002 and Haapaniemi et al., 2001.

claim: Via volume conduction, cardiac activity can be captured in both invasive and non-invasive recordings of neural activity.
source: Furthermore, it is well-known that, via volume conduction, cardiac activity can also be captured in both invasive and non-invasive recordings of neural activity (Dirlich et al., 1997; Jousmäki and Hari, 1996; Kern et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Dirlich et al., 1997; Jousmäki and Hari, 1996; Kern et al., 2013.

claim: It is considered best practice to measure and remove cardiac activity from M/EEG recordings.
source: Hence, it is also considered best practice to measure and remove cardiac activity from M/EEG recordings (Gross et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gross et al., 2013.

claim: Only 17.1% of EEG studies explicitly mention that cardiac activity was removed.
source: This analysis revealed that only 17.1% of EEG studies explicitly mention that cardiac activity was removed
evidence: This is based on the literature analysis conducted by the authors and shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: Only 16.5% of EEG studies measure ECG.
source: and only 16.5% measure ECG
evidence: This is based on the literature analysis conducted by the authors and shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: 45.9% of MEG studies removed cardiac activity.
source: 45.9% of MEG studies removed cardiac activity
evidence: This is based on the literature analysis conducted by the authors and shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: 31.1% of MEG studies mention that ECG was measured.
source: and 31.1% of MEG studies mention that ECG was measured
evidence: This is based on the literature analysis conducted by the authors and shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: The most commonly applied method both in EEG and MEG recordings for removing cardiac activity was independent component analysis (ICA).
source: We found that the most commonly applied method both in EEG and MEG recordings was independent component analysis (ICA).
evidence: This is based on the literature analysis conducted by the authors and shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: The spectral slope of ECG flattened with age over a vast amount of different frequency ranges.
source: Our results show that the spectral slope flattened with age over a vast amount of different frequency ranges (see Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the analysis of ECG data across 4 datasets, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: An age-related steepening of the spectral slope was noted in one dataset (ECG Dataset 3 - CamCAN) in the low-frequency range (0.25–12 Hz).
source: However, we also noted an age-related steepening of the spectral slope in one dataset (ECG Dataset 3 - CamCAN) in the low-frequency range (0.25–12 Hz, see Discussion).
evidence: This is a finding from the ECG analysis of the CamCAN dataset.

claim: Spectral slopes in lower frequency ranges (0.25–20 Hz) were more consistently related to heart rate variability indices (39.4–74.6% of all investigated indices) than spectral slopes in higher frequency ranges (16–30.01% of all investigated indices).
source: Overall, spectral slopes in lower frequency ranges were more consistently related to heart rate variability indices (39.4–74.6% percent of all investigated indices) than spectral slopes in higher frequency ranges (16–30.01% percent of all investigated indices; see Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on the exploratory analysis relating spectral slopes to 90 HRV indices, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: If ECG components are not removed via ICA, the ECG signal is captured equally strong at zero-time lags both in EEG and MEG recordings.
source: Our results show that if ECG components are not removed via ICA, the ECG signal is captured equally strong at zero-time lags both in EEG and MEG recordings (see Figure 3A,C,D).
evidence: This is based on the temporal response function analysis shown in Figure 3A,C,D.

claim: After removing ECG-related components from the data, TRF peaks emerged (although reduced) at zero-time lags in EEG, but not in MEG recordings.
source: Even after removing ECG-related components from the data, TRF peaks emerged (although reduced) at zero-time lags in EEG, but not in MEG recordings (see Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is based on the temporal response function analysis shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Reconstruction (decoding) of the ECG signal was reduced, but remained above chance even after rejecting the ICA signal using ECG both in MEG and EEG recordings.
source: Furthermore, reconstruction (decoding) of the ECG signal was reduced, but remained above chance even after rejecting the ICA signal using ECG both in MEG and EEG recordings (r>0).
evidence: This is based on the decoding analysis of ECG from M/EEG data.

claim: The presence of the ECG signal was more pronounced in EEG compared to MEG recordings, after removing ECG-related components.
source: Interestingly, the presence of the ECG signal was more pronounced in EEG compared to MEG recordings, after removing ECG-related components (βstandardized (EEG > MEG)=0.97, HDI = [0.42, 1.52]; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of residual ECG activity in EEG vs MEG, shown in Figure 3D.

claim: ECG-related components extracted from MEG recordings were more related to the ECG signal than the components extracted from the EEG.
source: Additionally, ECG-related components extracted from MEG recordings were more related to the ECG signal than the components extracted from the EEG (βstandardized (EEG > MEG)=–0.76, HDI = [-1.35,–0.18]; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of ECG component correlations in MEG vs EEG, shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Neural and cardiac activity are more difficult to separate in EEG as opposed to MEG recordings.
source: These results show that (A) residual ECG activity remains in surface neural recordings, even after applying a very sensitive threshold to detect and remove ECG components via ICA and (B) neural and cardiac activity are more difficult to separate in EEG as opposed to MEG recordings
evidence: This is inferred from the TRF and reconstruction analyses showing more residual ECG in EEG.

claim: Over a broad amount of individual fitting ranges and sensors, aging resulted in a steepening of spectral slopes across conditions with 'steepening effects' observed in 25% of the slope fits in MEGECG not rejected, 0.5% in MEGECG rejected, and 60% for MEGECG components.
source: This analysis, which is depicted in Figure 4, shows that over a broad amount of individual fitting ranges and sensors, aging resulted in a steepening of spectral slopes across conditions (see Figure 4B) with 'steepening effects' observed in 25% of the slope fits in MEGECG not rejected, 0.5% in MEGECG rejected, and 60% for MEGECG components.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the MEG analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: 'Flattening effects' in the spectral slope were found in 0.16% of the processing options in MEGECG not rejected, 0.3% in MEGECG rejected, and 0.46% in MEGECG components.
source: However, we also found 'flattening effects' in the spectral slope for 0.16% of the processing options in MEGECG not rejected, 0.3% in MEGECG rejected, and 0.46% in MEGECG components.
evidence: This is a finding from the MEG analysis across different processing options.

claim: Both flattening and steepening effects were most frequently observed on the MEGECG components.
source: Interestingly, this analysis shows that overall options, both flattening and steepening effects were most frequently observed on the MEGECG components.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of effect frequencies across conditions.

claim: A vast majority of observed effects, irrespective of condition, show a steepening of the spectral slope with age across sensors and frequency ranges.
source: This analysis also indicates that a vast majority of observed effects, irrespective of condition (ECG components, ECG not rejected, ECG rejected), show a steepening of the spectral slope with age across sensors and frequency ranges.
evidence: This is a summary finding from the MEG analysis.

claim: Age-related flattening in spectral slopes occurred mainly at centrally and parietally located electrodes in lower frequency ranges between 0.5 and 45 Hz.
source: However, despite the large amount of age-related steepening effects, we also noted age-related flattening in spectral slopes that occurred mainly at centrally and parietally located electrodes in lower frequency ranges between 0.5 and 45 Hz (see Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from the MEG analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: These results overlap both in frequency range and recording site with some of the results previously reported in the literature.
source: Importantly, these results overlap both in frequency range and recording site with some of the results previously reported in the literature (Voytek et al., 2015; Tröndle et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous findings supported by citations.

claim: Age-related flattening of the spectral slope is tied to specific recording sites and frequency ranges.
source: This suggests that age-related flattening of the spectral slope is tied to specific recording sites and frequency ranges.
evidence: This is inferred from the spatial and frequency-specific patterns of flattening effects.

claim: When adding both MEGECG component and MEGECG rejected as predictors, age-related flattening effects were reduced, yielding no longer significant flattening results.
source: The analysis revealed that when adding both MEGECG component and MEGECG rejected as predictors, age-related flattening effects were reduced, yielding no longer significant flattening results (see Figure 4B; upper panel).
evidence: This is based on the multiple regression analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In case of the observed steepening effects, significant effects for MEGECG components remained in 98.75% of the tested frequency ranges.
source: However, in case of the observed steepening effects, significant effects for MEGECG components remained in 98.75% of the tested frequency ranges (see Figure 4B; lower panel).
evidence: This is based on the multiple regression analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Whether or not aperiodic brain activity changes independently from cardiac activity with age depends on the recording site and the selected frequency range.
source: In sum, these results suggest that whether or not aperiodic brain activity changes independently from cardiac activity with age depends on the recording site and the selected frequency range.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the multiple regression analyses.

claim: The spectral slope of the ECG signal was significantly flatter during the 'Delay' compared to the 'Baseline' period in the working memory task.
source: The spectral slope of the ECG signal was significantly flatter during the 'Delay' compared to the 'Baseline' period (D).
evidence: This is a finding from the working memory analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The flattening of the spectral slope relative to 'Baseline' was strongest in conditions with higher working memory load.
source: The flattening of the spectral slope relative to 'Baseline' was strongest in conditions with higher working memory load.
evidence: This is a finding from the working memory analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The slope flattened the most in the condition with the highest working memory load (13 items; βstandardized=0.42, HDI = [0.33, 0.52]).
source: The slope flattened the most in the condition with the highest working memory load (13 items; βstandardized=0.42, HDI = [0.33, 0.52])
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the working memory analysis.

claim: Previous research has shown scaling differences in the spectral slope between MEG and EEG recordings.
source: Previous research has shown scaling differences in the spectral slope between MEG and EEG recordings (Dehghani et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dehghani et al., 2010.

claim: These scaling differences are partly widespread (overall flatter sloped spectra in MEG data) and partly regionally specific (steeper sloped spectra at vertex in MEG compared to EEG recordings and vice versa at frontal regions).
source: These scaling differences are partly widespread (overall flatter sloped spectra in MEG data) and partly regionally specific (steeper sloped spectra at vertex in MEG compared to EEG recordings and vice versa at frontal regions).
evidence: This is based on citation to Dehghani et al., 2010.

claim: Magnetic field recordings are not distorted by the tissue conductivity of the scalp, skull, cerebrospinal fluid, and brain.
source: This differently affects the signal recorded using MEG and EEG, as magnetic field recordings are not distorted by the tissue conductivity of the scalp, skull, cerebrospinal fluid, and brain (Singh, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Singh, 2014.

claim: EEG typically integrates activity over larger volumes than MEG, resulting in differently shaped spectra across both recording methods.
source: Bénar et al., 2019 demonstrate that EEG typically integrates activity over larger volumes than MEG, resulting in differently shaped spectra across both recording methods.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bénar et al., 2019.

claim: During aging, both changes in conductive tissue properties and functional connectivity occur.
source: During aging, both changes in conductive tissue properties (Mohammed et al., 2017; Thomas et al., 2018) and functional connectivity occur (Deery et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mohammed et al., 2017; Thomas et al., 2018; and Deery et al., 2023.

claim: Separating ECG-related components from neural activity using ICA seems to work worse in EEG compared to MEG recordings.
source: Furthermore, separating ECG-related components from neural activity using ICA seems to work worse in EEG compared to MEG recordings (see Figure 3A-D).
evidence: This is inferred from the TRF analysis showing more residual ECG in EEG after ICA.

claim: Previous work has shown that a linked mastoid reference alone was particularly effective in reducing the impact of ECG-related activity on aperiodic activity measured using EEG.
source: Previous work (Kozhemiako et al., 2022; Lendner et al., 2020) has shown that a linked mastoid reference alone was particularly effective in reducing the impact of ECG-related activity on aperiodic activity measured using EEG.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kozhemiako et al., 2022 and Lendner et al., 2020.

claim: Linked mastoid referencing can distort temporal activity.
source: Linked mastoid referencing, for instance, can distort temporal activity (Feindel et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Feindel et al., 2009.

claim: The aperiodic signal recorded non-invasively originates from multiple physiological sources.
source: These findings underscore the complexity of analyzing aperiodic activity, indicating that the aperiodic signal recorded non-invasively originates from multiple physiological sources.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analyses showing both cardiac and neural contributions.

claim: Neural and vascular processes are known to interact with each other.
source: In fact, neural and vascular processes are known to interact with each other (Takarada-Iemata et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Takarada-Iemata et al., 2019.

claim: A current popular hypothesis states that the generative process underlying aperiodic neural activity is mainly attributed to differences in the ratio between excitatory (AMPA) and inhibitory (GABA) currents that influence the slope of the neural power spectrum.
source: For example, a current popular hypothesis states that the generative process underlying aperiodic neural activity is mainly attributed to differences in the ratio between excitatory (AMPA) and inhibitory (GABA) currents that influence the slope of the neural power spectrum (Gao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gao et al., 2017.

claim: Excitatory currents such as AMPA decay faster than inhibitory currents like GABA.
source: Excitatory currents such as AMPA decay faster than inhibitory currents like GABA.
evidence: This is established knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: Flatter power spectra may be indicative of the presence of more excitatory than inhibitory currents and vice versa (steeper sloped power spectra).
source: This means that flatter power spectra may be indicative of the presence of more excitatory than inhibitory currents and vice versa (steeper sloped power spectra Gao et al., 2017).

source: This theory is (in part) based on research showing that GABAergic drugs like propofol (Gao et al., 2017)

claim: Glutamatergic drugs like ketamine modulate the slope of electrophysiologically measured power spectra.
source: and glutamatergic drugs like ketamine (Waschke et al., 2021) modulate the slope of electrophysiologically measured power spectra.

source: However, propofol and ketamine not only influence neural activity, but also influence heart rate variability (a core component of the ECG Goddard et al., 2021; Kanaya et al., 2003).

source: Previous work has shown that propofol-induced changes to the spectral slope were still present in EEG recordings after using ICA to reject ECG components from the data (Lendner et al., 2020).

claim: Cardiac activity remains in EEG signals even after separating cardiac from neural sources using an ICA with a very sensitive rejection criterion.

claim: It is plausible that drug-induced effects on aperiodic 'neural' activity can still be conflated by cardiac activity.
source: It is therefore plausible that drug-induced effects on aperiodic 'neural' activity can still be conflated by cardiac activity.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the finding of residual ECG in EEG after ICA.

claim: Muscle activity can be captured in (non-)invasive recordings and may drastically influence measures of the spectral slope.

claim: Head movements increased significantly with aging.

claim: Previously suspected periodic age-related changes in alpha power may actually be attributable to differences in aperiodic activity.
source: This has, for instance, revealed that previously suspected periodic age-related changes in alpha power may actually be attributable to differences in aperiodic activity (Donoghue et al., 2020; Merkin et al., 2023).

claim: Cardiac activity is also captured on ECoG.
source: Given that cardiac activity is also captured on, for example ECoG (Kern et al., 2013)

source: Changes in aperiodic activity of peripheral and neural signals are co-modulated by similar traits, states, and disorders.
